title: Grade 4 ISLAMIC RELIGIOUS EDUCATION — 3.3 Prophets mentioned in the Qur’an

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Allah sent prophets to guide people, and the Qur’an names twenty-five of them. In this sub-strand you will learn those names, study their virtues of patience, honesty, truthfulness, generosity and obedience, and practise the same virtues in your own day.

## Strand 3.0: Pillars of Iman
Sub-strand 3.3: Prophets mentioned in the Qur’an
Suggested lessons: 6

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) mention the twenty-five prophets of Allah (S.W.T.) in the Qur’an
b) analyse the virtues of the prophets of Allah for character formation
c) apply the virtues of the prophets of Allah in their daily life
d) acknowledge the belief in the prophets of Allah as a Pillar of Iman

## What this sub-strand covers
• Virtues of the Prophets (patience, honesty, truthfulness, generosity and obedience)

## Key inquiry questions
1. What virtues do we learn from these prophets?

## Core competencies
• Communication and collaboration: the skills of speaking and writing are enhanced as learners name the prophets of Allah and write them in their notebook.
• Creativity and imagination: the skill is enhanced as learners dramatise/role-play how they can apply the virtues of the prophets of Allah in their daily life.
• Citizenship: social and civic skills are enhanced as learners discuss the virtues (patience, honesty, truthfulness, generosity and obedience) of the prophets, in pairs or small groups.

## Values
• Social justice equity enhanced as learners dramatise/role-play how they can apply the virtues of the prophets in their daily life.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Self-esteem as learners name prophets mentioned in the Qur’an.

## Links to other learning areas
• Social Studies: as learners discuss the virtues exhibited by the prophets of Allah S.W.T., which is related to good governance.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Islamic Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 3.0 Pillars of Iman, Sub-strand 3.3 Prophets mentioned in the Qur’an
• Qur’an 2:285, 4:163-165, 6:84-86, 21:83-88, 29:14, 33:40, 37:102-107 and 51:24-27
• Sahih al-Bukhari: the Prophet (S.A.W.) was the most generous of people, and even more so in Ramadan

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Who the prophets are

LESSON 1: WHO THE PROPHETS ARE
==============================

## What you will learn
• Explain what a prophet is.
• State that belief in the prophets is a pillar of Iman.
• Begin the list of the twenty-five prophets with the earliest names.

Curriculum outcomes: a) mention the twenty-five prophets of Allah (S.W.T.) in the Qur’an; d) acknowledge the belief in the prophets of Allah as a Pillar of Iman

## Introduction
Some learners in your class may be called Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa or Muhammad. Those names belong first to prophets of Allah. Believing in all of them is a pillar of Iman.

## Notes
### What a prophet is
A prophet is a person chosen by Allah to receive His message and to guide people. A rasul, or messenger, is sent with a revealed law or book, or to a people. Every messenger is a prophet. Prophets are human beings. They eat, sleep and walk in the markets, and they do not lie or betray the message. They are the best of people, and they are protected from teaching falsehood about Allah.

### A pillar of Iman
Belief in the prophets is one of the pillars of Iman. A Muslim believes in all of them, from the first to the last. We do not accept some and reject others. The Qur’an praises those who say they make no distinction, in belief, between any of Allah’s messengers (Qur’an 2:285). Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last of them, the seal of the prophets (Qur’an 33:40). No prophet comes after him.

### Names to start with
The Qur’an mentions twenty-five prophets by name in the passages Muslims use for this list, including Qur’an 4:163-165, 6:84-86 and 21:85-88, together with other verses that name Adam, Hud, Salih and Shuayb. The earliest in the list you will memorise are Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih.

Adam (alayhis-salam) was the first human being and the first prophet. Nuh (alayhis-salam) called his people for a very long time. The Qur’an says he remained among them for a thousand years minus fifty years (Qur’an 29:14). Hud was sent to the people of Ad, and Salih was sent to the people of Thamud.

Look around the class. If a learner carries one of these names, that name is a reminder of a prophet, and it should be used with respect.

## Key words
• prophet (nabi) — a person chosen by Allah to guide people with His message
• messenger (rasul) — a prophet sent with Allah’s message to a people
• seal of the prophets — the last prophet, Muhammad (S.A.W.)

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner says, “I believe in Muhammad only, not in Musa or Isa.” Which pillar has he broken?

Working:
1. Belief in all the prophets is a pillar of Iman.
2. The Qur’an forbids accepting some messengers and rejecting others.
3. Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last, and the earlier prophets are also believed in.

Answer: He has left out part of the pillar of belief in the prophets. A Muslim believes in all of them.

## Activity: Names of prophets in our class
You will need: Notebook, A list of the first five names on the board
1. With respect, identify learners who are named after prophets, such as Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa or Muhammad.
2. Write the five names Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih in your notebook.
3. Beside each name that you already know, write one true fact from the lesson.
4. Say together: we believe in all the prophets, and Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last.

## Practice
1. What is a prophet?
2. Who is the last prophet?
3. Name the first five prophets in the list you are learning.
4. How long does the Qur’an say Nuh remained among his people?

## Summary
• A prophet is a human being chosen by Allah to guide people.
• Belief in all the prophets is a pillar of Iman.
• Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last prophet. The list begins Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih.

### Answers to practice
1. A person chosen by Allah to receive His message and guide people.
2. Muhammad (S.A.W.), the seal of the prophets.
3. Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih.
4. A thousand years minus fifty years.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: From Ibrahim to Yusuf

LESSON 2: FROM IBRAHIM TO YUSUF
===============================

## What you will learn
• Name the prophets from Ibrahim to Yusuf.
• Keep the growing list in order.
• Recall one sure fact about Ibrahim, Musa’s family line, or Yusuf without mixing up their stories.

Curriculum outcomes: a) mention the twenty-five prophets of Allah (S.W.T.) in the Qur’an

## Introduction
Ibrahim (alayhis-salam) is a father of prophets. From his family came messengers whose names you already hear in dua and in the Qur’an. This lesson adds them to the list of twenty-five.

## Notes
### The next names
After Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih, learn these prophets in order:

6. Ibrahim
7. Lut
8. Ismail
9. Ishaq
10. Yaqub
11. Yusuf

Ibrahim (alayhis-salam) called people to worship Allah alone and broke the habit of idol worship. He is called Khalilullah, the close friend of Allah. Lut (alayhis-salam) was sent to a people who rejected Allah’s limits. Ismail (alayhis-salam) and Ishaq (alayhis-salam) were sons of Ibrahim. Yaqub (alayhis-salam) was the son of Ishaq, and Yusuf (alayhis-salam) was the son of Yaqub.

### A fact you can be sure of
The Qur’an tells the story of Yusuf: his brothers wronged him, Allah raised him in Egypt, and he later forgave his brothers and provided for them. That story is a full surah, Surat Yusuf. You do not need every detail yet. You do need his name in the list, and the lesson that he remained truthful under hardship.

Qur’an 6:84-86 mentions Ibrahim’s descendants among the guided: Ishaq, Yaqub, and later Yusuf among other prophets. Write the eleven names you now have, from Adam to Yusuf, until you can say them without looking. The remaining fourteen come in the next lesson. Do not skip a name, because the outcome is to mention all twenty-five.

## Key words
• Khalilullah — the close friend of Allah, a title of Ibrahim (alayhis-salam)
• alayhis-salam — peace be upon him; said after a prophet’s name

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put these six names in the order used in class: Yusuf, Ibrahim, Ismail, Lut, Yaqub, Ishaq.

Working:
1. Ibrahim comes first among them.
2. Then Lut, then Ibrahim’s sons Ismail and Ishaq.
3. Then Yaqub, then Yusuf.

Answer: Ibrahim, Lut, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, Yusuf.

## Activity: Write the prophets from Adam to Yusuf
You will need: Notebook, Name cards for the eleven prophets
1. Arrange the cards from Adam to Yusuf.
2. Check the order with the verses your teacher points to in Qur’an 6:84-86 and with the class list.
3. Each learner writes the eleven names in the notebook.
4. Say the list aloud twice as a group.

## Practice
1. Who is called Khalilullah?
2. Name the two sons of Ibrahim included in the list of prophets.
3. Whose son was Yusuf?
4. Recite the eleven names from Adam to Yusuf in order.

## Summary
• Ibrahim, Lut, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub and Yusuf follow the first five prophets.
• Ismail and Ishaq were sons of Ibrahim, Yaqub was the son of Ishaq, and Yusuf was the son of Yaqub.
• The list from Adam to Yusuf has eleven names.

### Answers to practice
1. Ibrahim (alayhis-salam).
2. Ismail and Ishaq.
3. Yusuf was the son of Yaqub.
4. Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, Yusuf.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: From Ayyub to Muhammad (S.A.W.)

LESSON 3: FROM AYYUB TO MUHAMMAD (S.A.W.)
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Name the prophets from Ayyub to Muhammad (S.A.W.).
• Recite all twenty-five names.
• Acknowledge belief in every prophet, with Muhammad as the last.

Curriculum outcomes: a) mention the twenty-five prophets of Allah (S.W.T.) in the Qur’an; d) acknowledge the belief in the prophets of Allah as a Pillar of Iman

## Introduction
The second half of the list includes Musa, Dawud, Sulayman, Isa and Muhammad (S.A.W.). When these fourteen names join the first eleven, the twenty-five are complete.

## Notes
### The remaining prophets
Continue the list in this order:

12. Ayyub
13. Shuayb
14. Musa
15. Harun
16. Dhul-Kifl
17. Dawud
18. Sulayman
19. Ilyas
20. Al-Yasa
21. Yunus
22. Zakariyya
23. Yahya
24. Isa
25. Muhammad (S.A.W.)

Musa (alayhis-salam) was sent to Fir’awn and was given the Tawrah. Allah spoke to him, as Qur’an 4:164 states. Harun was his brother and a prophet with him. Dawud was given the Zabur (Qur’an 4:163). Sulayman was the son of Dawud and a prophet-king. Yunus (alayhis-salam), also called Dhul-Nun, called on Allah from inside the fish. Zakariyya was the father of Yahya. Isa (alayhis-salam), the son of Maryam, is a prophet and messenger. He is not the son of Allah. Surat Al-Ikhlas has already taught that Allah does not beget.

Shuayb, Dhul-Kifl, Ilyas and Al-Yasa are also among the twenty-five. Do not drop their names because the stories are shorter in class.

### The full belief
Say the twenty-five names until they are firm. Believe in every one of them. Love them and follow the message as completed by Muhammad (S.A.W.). We say “alayhis-salam” after the earlier prophets and “Sallallahu alayhi wa sallam” after Muhammad. Rejecting Isa, or calling him God, both contradict this pillar. He is a honoured prophet of Allah, and Muhammad is the last messenger.

## Key words
• Tawrah — the scripture given to Musa (alayhis-salam)
• Zabur — the scripture given to Dawud (alayhis-salam)
• Sallallahu alayhi wa sallam — may Allah send prayers and peace upon him; said after the name of Prophet Muhammad

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A classmate says Isa is the son of Allah, and another says Isa was not a prophet. How does the list of twenty-five correct both sentences?

Working:
1. Isa is prophet number 24 in the class list. He is a true prophet.
2. Allah has no children, as Surat Al-Ikhlas teaches.
3. Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the twenty-fifth and the last.

Answer: Isa is a prophet of Allah, not His son. We believe in him and in Muhammad (S.A.W.) as the final prophet.

## Activity: Write all twenty-five names
You will need: Notebook, The references Qur’an 4:163-165, 6:84-86 and 21:85-88 as the teacher reads the names
1. Listen as the teacher reads the prophets named in those passages.
2. Write all twenty-five names in order in your notebook.
3. Cover the page and, in pairs, test each other on any five names.
4. End by stating that belief in all of them is a pillar of Iman and that Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last.

## Practice
1. Who was given the Tawrah, and who was given the Zabur?
2. Where does Isa stand in the list, and who comes after him?
3. Name Dhul-Kifl’s place among these prophets: is he included in the twenty-five?
4. How many prophets are in the full list?

## Summary
• The list ends with Ayyub, Shuayb, Musa, Harun, Dhul-Kifl, Dawud, Sulayman, Ilyas, Al-Yasa, Yunus, Zakariyya, Yahya, Isa and Muhammad (S.A.W.).
• There are twenty-five prophets to mention.
• We believe in all of them, and Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the seal of the prophets.

### Answers to practice
1. Musa was given the Tawrah, and Dawud was given the Zabur.
2. Isa is the twenty-fourth. Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the twenty-fifth and the last.
3. Yes. Dhul-Kifl is one of the twenty-five prophets.
4. Twenty-five.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Patience and obedience of the prophets

LESSON 4: PATIENCE AND OBEDIENCE OF THE PROPHETS
================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain patience using the examples of Nuh and Ayyub.
• Explain obedience using Ibrahim and Yunus.
• Write the meaning of each virtue in a notebook sentence.

Curriculum outcomes: b) analyse the virtues of the prophets of Allah for character formation

## Introduction
The prophets were not guides only because of miracles. They were guides because of character. Two of their virtues are patience when the road is long, and obedience when the command is hard.

## Notes
### Patience
Sabr means staying firm on what is right, without giving up and without complaining against Allah. Nuh (alayhis-salam) called his people to Allah for a thousand years minus fifty, and most of them still refused (Qur’an 29:14). He did not abandon the message. Ayyub (alayhis-salam) was tested with serious illness and loss. He called on his Lord and remained patient. The Qur’an says Allah answered him and removed the harm (Qur’an 21:83-84).

Patience is not silence in the face of bullying that you should report. It is firmness: you keep praying, you keep telling the truth, and you do not insult Allah because a week has been difficult.

### Obedience
The prophets obeyed Allah even when the command cost them comfort. Ibrahim (alayhis-salam) was tested with a command about his son. The son, understanding the dream his father had been shown, said that his father should do what he was commanded, and Allah ransomed the son with a great sacrifice (Qur’an 37:102-107). That obedience is remembered at Eid al-Adha.

Yunus (alayhis-salam) left his people without waiting as he should have. He was swallowed by the fish. Inside it he obeyed by turning back to Allah with the words: there is no god but You, glory be to You, I have been among the wrongdoers (Qur’an 21:87). Allah saved him. Obedience includes coming back as soon as you know you were wrong.

Write both virtues in your own words and attach one prophet to each, so the story and the virtue stay together.

## Key words
• sabr — patience; remaining firm in obedience to Allah
• obedience — doing what Allah has commanded

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner has invited a classmate to salah for many days and feels like stopping. Which prophet’s patience speaks to this moment?

Working:
1. Nuh continued his call for a very long time.
2. The learner’s few days are small beside that patience.
3. He continues kindly, without insulting the classmate.

Answer: Nuh (alayhis-salam). The learner keeps inviting kindly and does not give up at once.

## Activity: Describe patience and obedience
You will need: Notebook, Verses read by the teacher: Qur’an 21:83-84, 21:87, 29:14 and 37:102-107
1. In pairs, describe the patience of Nuh and of Ayyub in two or three sentences.
2. Describe the obedience of Ibrahim and his son, and the return of Yunus to Allah.
3. Write the points in your notebook under the headings Patience and Obedience.
4. Read one point to the class.

## Practice
1. How did Ayyub show patience?
2. What did Yunus say when he turned back to Allah from inside the fish?
3. What virtue did Ibrahim and his son show when Ibrahim was tested?

## Summary
• Nuh and Ayyub are models of patience.
• Ibrahim and his son obeyed Allah in a hard test, and Yunus obeyed by turning back.
• Patience and obedience are virtues for character, not only stories.

### Answers to practice
1. He remained patient during serious illness and called on Allah, who removed the harm.
2. There is no god but You. Glory be to You. Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.
3. Obedience. The son told his father to do what Allah had commanded.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: Honesty, truthfulness and generosity

LESSON 5: HONESTY, TRUTHFULNESS AND GENEROSITY
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain honesty and truthfulness from the lives of the prophets.
• Explain generosity from Ibrahim and Muhammad (S.A.W.).
• Separate a true virtue from a similar bad habit.

Curriculum outcomes: b) analyse the virtues of the prophets of Allah for character formation

## Introduction
People trusted the prophets with news from Allah because the prophets did not lie about small things. They also gave freely. Honesty, truthfulness and generosity are the next virtues to learn.

## Notes
### Honesty and truthfulness
Honesty means dealing fairly: you do not steal, cheat in measure, or take a hidden advantage. Truthfulness means your words match the facts. All the prophets were truthful. Their people sometimes rejected the message, but they could not prove that the prophet was a liar in his character.

Muhammad (S.A.W.) was called As-Sadiq Al-Amin, the truthful and trustworthy, before prophethood. Yusuf (alayhis-salam) was trusted with the storehouses of Egypt because the king saw that he was knowledgeable and trustworthy. A prophet does not pass an exam by cheating or sell goods by hiding a fault.

### Generosity
Generosity is giving freely what is lawful to give. Ibrahim (alayhis-salam) hurried to prepare food when guests came to him (Qur’an 51:24-27). He did not wait to be pushed. Muhammad (S.A.W.) was the most generous of people, and he was even more generous in Ramadan (Bukhari). He did not love hoarding.

### Do not mix the virtue with a fault
Truthfulness is not the same as saying a hurtful thing for fun and then claiming “I was only honest”. Honesty does not cancel kindness. Generosity is not giving away someone else’s property, and it is not wasting. A generous learner shares a pencil, gives from what a parent allows, and still leaves enough for his or her own need. Write one clear sentence for each virtue so that you can use it in the role-play of the next lesson.

## Key words
• honesty — dealing fairly and not taking what is not yours
• truthfulness — saying what is true
• generosity — giving freely from what is lawful

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A seller of mangoes hides the rotten ones under the good ones. Which virtue of the prophets has he broken, and what would Yusuf’s example suggest?

Working:
1. Hiding a fault in a sale is dishonest.
2. The prophets were trustworthy in their dealings.
3. He should show the fruit as it is or remove the rotten ones.

Answer: He has broken honesty. A prophetic example is to deal in a way people can trust.

## Activity: Three virtues on paper
You will need: Notebook
1. In small groups, discuss honesty, truthfulness and generosity using the prophets named in the lesson.
2. Write one sentence for each virtue and one prophet beside it.
3. Add one school example that is really the virtue, and reject one example that only pretends to be.
4. Read your sentences to another group.

## Practice
1. What titles did people give Muhammad (S.A.W.) that show truthfulness and trust?
2. How did Ibrahim show generosity to his guests?
3. Why is sharing another person’s pencil without permission not generosity?

## Summary
• The prophets were honest and truthful, and people could trust their dealings.
• Ibrahim fed his guests quickly, and Muhammad (S.A.W.) was most generous, especially in Ramadan.
• Kind truthfulness and lawful giving are the real virtues.

### Answers to practice
1. As-Sadiq, the Truthful, and Al-Amin, the Trustworthy.
2. He hurried to prepare food for them.
3. Generosity gives what you may lawfully give. Taking someone else’s property is not giving.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Practising the virtues of the prophets

LESSON 6: PRACTISING THE VIRTUES OF THE PROPHETS
================================================

## What you will learn
• Role-play patience, honesty, truthfulness, generosity and obedience.
• Choose one virtue to practise this week.
• State again that belief in the prophets is a pillar of Iman.

Curriculum outcomes: b) analyse the virtues of the prophets of Allah for character formation; c) apply the virtues of the prophets of Allah in their daily life; d) acknowledge the belief in the prophets of Allah as a Pillar of Iman

## Introduction
A virtue that stays inside a notebook has not yet formed character. The prophets’ patience, honesty, truthfulness, generosity and obedience are for the corridor, the market and the kitchen, not only for a test.

## Notes
### From story to action
Apply each virtue in a way that fits your age:

- Patience: keep learning a surah that is taking time. Do not tear the page or insult yourself. Ask for help and continue, as Nuh continued and as Ayyub remained firm.
- Obedience: do the halal thing your parent or teacher asks when it does not contradict Allah. If you slipped, return quickly, as Yunus returned to Allah with dua.
- Honesty: give back extra change. Do not hide a fault in something you sell or swap.
- Truthfulness: tell the teacher what actually happened when a window breaks. As-Sadiq did not invent a story.
- Generosity: share food or a skill. Explain a sum to a classmate who is stuck.

### Belief that changes behaviour
Acknowledging the prophets as a pillar of Iman means you mention all twenty-five with respect, you refuse to mock any of them, and you try to wear their virtues. Saying “I believe in Musa” while cheating, or “I love Ibrahim” while refusing to share, leaves the belief unfinished. The pillar is in the heart, and the virtues show it in the limbs.

Choose one virtue for seven days. Tell a partner the exact action. At the end of the week, be honest about whether you did it. If you failed on one day, obey Allah by starting again the next morning. That second start is itself a prophetic lesson.

## Key words
• apply — to put a virtue into a real action
• character formation — building steady good habits

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You accidentally break a friend’s ruler and feel like saying the desk broke it. Which virtue, and which prophetic title, correct you?

Working:
1. Truthfulness means the words match the facts.
2. The Prophet (S.A.W.) was As-Sadiq.
3. You apologise and offer to replace the ruler if you can.

Answer: Truthfulness, following As-Sadiq. Admit the break and make it right.

## Activity: Role-play the five virtues
You will need: Five situation cards: a hard surah, a parent’s lawful instruction, extra change, a broken ruler, a classmate without a pencil
1. In groups, pick one card and act the wrong response, then the prophetic response.
2. The class names the virtue: patience, obedience, honesty, truthfulness or generosity.
3. Each learner writes the virtue he or she will practise this week and the exact action.
4. Close by reciting the number of prophets, twenty-five, and stating that belief in them is a pillar of Iman.

## Practice
1. Give one way to practise patience with schoolwork.
2. Give one way to practise generosity without money.
3. Why is mocking any prophet against this pillar?
4. How many prophets must you be able to mention?

## Summary
• Patience, obedience, honesty, truthfulness and generosity can be practised at school.
• Belief in the prophets shows in respect for all twenty-five and in these virtues.
• If you fail one day, start again the next day.

### Answers to practice
1. Keep learning a difficult surah or sum, ask for help, and do not give up in anger.
2. Explain a lesson to a classmate or share time and learning materials.
3. Belief in all the prophets is a pillar of Iman, so every prophet is mentioned with respect.
4. Twenty-five.

REVISION QUIZ — 3.3 PROPHETS MENTIONED IN THE QUR’AN
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. How many prophets are named in the list you learned?
   A. Five
   B. Twelve
   C. Twenty-five
   D. One hundred

2. Who is the first prophet in the list, and who is the last?
   A. Musa and Isa
   B. Adam and Muhammad (S.A.W.)
   C. Ibrahim and Yusuf
   D. Nuh and Hud

3. Which statement about Isa (alayhis-salam) matches the pillar of Iman?
   A. He is the son of Allah
   B. He is not a prophet
   C. He is a prophet of Allah, and Allah has no children
   D. He came after Muhammad (S.A.W.)

4. Who was given the Zabur?
   A. Dawud
   B. Yunus
   C. Hud
   D. Salih

5. Nuh’s long call to his people is an example of which virtue?
   A. envy
   B. patience
   C. gambling
   D. showing off

6. Ayyub (alayhis-salam) is remembered especially for patience during which test?

7. Ibrahim hurrying to feed his guests is an example of which virtue?
   A. generosity
   B. falling asleep in salah
   C. hiding a fault in a sale
   D. rejecting messengers

8. Which action applies truthfulness at school?
   A. Blaming the desk for something you broke
   B. Telling the teacher what really happened
   C. Copying and saying the work is yours
   D. Hiding extra change

9. What does Yunus turning to Allah from inside the fish teach?
   A. that a sin cannot be followed by dua
   B. obedience in returning to Allah
   C. that the fish was a prophet
   D. that we may leave every duty

10. Belief in the prophets means…

11. Which group is in the correct order?
   A. Yusuf, Yaqub, Ishaq, Ibrahim
   B. Ibrahim, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, Yusuf
   C. Muhammad, Isa, Adam
   D. Hud, Musa, Adam, Nuh
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 3.3 PROPHETS MENTIONED IN THE QUR’AN
========================================

1. C. Twenty-five
   The Grade 4 list has twenty-five prophets, ending with Muhammad (S.A.W.).

2. B. Adam and Muhammad (S.A.W.)
   Adam is the first human and the first prophet. Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the seal of the prophets.

3. C. He is a prophet of Allah, and Allah has no children
   Isa is honoured as a prophet. Surat Al-Ikhlas teaches that Allah does not beget.

4. A. Dawud
   Qur’an 4:163 says Dawud was given the Zabur.

5. B. patience
   He remained among them for a thousand years minus fifty and did not abandon the message.

6. Serious illness, after which he called on Allah and Allah removed the harm.
   This is told in Qur’an 21:83-84.

7. A. generosity
   Qur’an 51:24-27 shows his generous welcome.

8. B. Telling the teacher what really happened
   Truthfulness means your words match the facts, as in the title As-Sadiq.

9. B. obedience in returning to Allah
   He admitted his fault and called on Allah, who saved him.

10. Believing in all twenty-five, respecting every one of them, and knowing that Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last.
   This belief is a pillar of Iman.

11. B. Ibrahim, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, Yusuf
   After Ibrahim come Lut, then Ismail and Ishaq, then Yaqub, then Yusuf. The option that keeps Ibrahim before his descendants is correct.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Allah sent prophets to guide people, and the Qur’an names twenty-five of them. In this sub-strand you will learn those names, study their virtues of patience, honesty, truthfulness, generosity and obedience, and practise the same virtues in your own day.

## Strand 3.0: Pillars of Iman
Sub-strand 3.3: Prophets mentioned in the Qur’an
Suggested lessons: 6

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) mention the twenty-five prophets of Allah (S.W.T.) in the Qur’an
b) analyse the virtues of the prophets of Allah for character formation
c) apply the virtues of the prophets of Allah in their daily life
d) acknowledge the belief in the prophets of Allah as a Pillar of Iman

## What this sub-strand covers
• Virtues of the Prophets (patience, honesty, truthfulness, generosity and obedience)

## Key inquiry questions
1. What virtues do we learn from these prophets?

## Core competencies
• Communication and collaboration: the skills of speaking and writing are enhanced as learners name the prophets of Allah and write them in their notebook.
• Creativity and imagination: the skill is enhanced as learners dramatise/role-play how they can apply the virtues of the prophets of Allah in their daily life.
• Citizenship: social and civic skills are enhanced as learners discuss the virtues (patience, honesty, truthfulness, generosity and obedience) of the prophets, in pairs or small groups.

## Values
• Social justice equity enhanced as learners dramatise/role-play how they can apply the virtues of the prophets in their daily life.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Self-esteem as learners name prophets mentioned in the Qur’an.

## Links to other learning areas
• Social Studies: as learners discuss the virtues exhibited by the prophets of Allah S.W.T., which is related to good governance.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Islamic Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 3.0 Pillars of Iman, Sub-strand 3.3 Prophets mentioned in the Qur’an
• Qur’an 2:285, 4:163-165, 6:84-86, 21:83-88, 29:14, 33:40, 37:102-107 and 51:24-27
• Sahih al-Bukhari: the Prophet (S.A.W.) was the most generous of people, and even more so in Ramadan

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Who the prophets are
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: WHO THE PROPHETS ARE
==============================

## What you will learn
• Explain what a prophet is.
• State that belief in the prophets is a pillar of Iman.
• Begin the list of the twenty-five prophets with the earliest names.

Curriculum outcomes: a) mention the twenty-five prophets of Allah (S.W.T.) in the Qur’an; d) acknowledge the belief in the prophets of Allah as a Pillar of Iman

## Introduction
Some learners in your class may be called Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa or Muhammad. Those names belong first to prophets of Allah. Believing in all of them is a pillar of Iman.

## Notes
### What a prophet is
A prophet is a person chosen by Allah to receive His message and to guide people. A rasul, or messenger, is sent with a revealed law or book, or to a people. Every messenger is a prophet. Prophets are human beings. They eat, sleep and walk in the markets, and they do not lie or betray the message. They are the best of people, and they are protected from teaching falsehood about Allah.

### A pillar of Iman
Belief in the prophets is one of the pillars of Iman. A Muslim believes in all of them, from the first to the last. We do not accept some and reject others. The Qur’an praises those who say they make no distinction, in belief, between any of Allah’s messengers (Qur’an 2:285). Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last of them, the seal of the prophets (Qur’an 33:40). No prophet comes after him.

### Names to start with
The Qur’an mentions twenty-five prophets by name in the passages Muslims use for this list, including Qur’an 4:163-165, 6:84-86 and 21:85-88, together with other verses that name Adam, Hud, Salih and Shuayb. The earliest in the list you will memorise are Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih.

Adam (alayhis-salam) was the first human being and the first prophet. Nuh (alayhis-salam) called his people for a very long time. The Qur’an says he remained among them for a thousand years minus fifty years (Qur’an 29:14). Hud was sent to the people of Ad, and Salih was sent to the people of Thamud.

Look around the class. If a learner carries one of these names, that name is a reminder of a prophet, and it should be used with respect.

## Key words
• prophet (nabi) — a person chosen by Allah to guide people with His message
• messenger (rasul) — a prophet sent with Allah’s message to a people
• seal of the prophets — the last prophet, Muhammad (S.A.W.)

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner says, “I believe in Muhammad only, not in Musa or Isa.” Which pillar has he broken?

Working:
1. Belief in all the prophets is a pillar of Iman.
2. The Qur’an forbids accepting some messengers and rejecting others.
3. Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last, and the earlier prophets are also believed in.

Answer: He has left out part of the pillar of belief in the prophets. A Muslim believes in all of them.

## Activity: Names of prophets in our class
You will need: Notebook, A list of the first five names on the board
1. With respect, identify learners who are named after prophets, such as Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa or Muhammad.
2. Write the five names Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih in your notebook.
3. Beside each name that you already know, write one true fact from the lesson.
4. Say together: we believe in all the prophets, and Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last.

## Practice
1. What is a prophet?
2. Who is the last prophet?
3. Name the first five prophets in the list you are learning.
4. How long does the Qur’an say Nuh remained among his people?

## Summary
• A prophet is a human being chosen by Allah to guide people.
• Belief in all the prophets is a pillar of Iman.
• Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last prophet. The list begins Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih.

### Answers to practice
1. A person chosen by Allah to receive His message and guide people.
2. Muhammad (S.A.W.), the seal of the prophets.
3. Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih.
4. A thousand years minus fifty years.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: From Ibrahim to Yusuf
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: FROM IBRAHIM TO YUSUF
===============================

## What you will learn
• Name the prophets from Ibrahim to Yusuf.
• Keep the growing list in order.
• Recall one sure fact about Ibrahim, Musa’s family line, or Yusuf without mixing up their stories.

Curriculum outcomes: a) mention the twenty-five prophets of Allah (S.W.T.) in the Qur’an

## Introduction
Ibrahim (alayhis-salam) is a father of prophets. From his family came messengers whose names you already hear in dua and in the Qur’an. This lesson adds them to the list of twenty-five.

## Notes
### The next names
After Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih, learn these prophets in order:

6. Ibrahim
7. Lut
8. Ismail
9. Ishaq
10. Yaqub
11. Yusuf

Ibrahim (alayhis-salam) called people to worship Allah alone and broke the habit of idol worship. He is called Khalilullah, the close friend of Allah. Lut (alayhis-salam) was sent to a people who rejected Allah’s limits. Ismail (alayhis-salam) and Ishaq (alayhis-salam) were sons of Ibrahim. Yaqub (alayhis-salam) was the son of Ishaq, and Yusuf (alayhis-salam) was the son of Yaqub.

### A fact you can be sure of
The Qur’an tells the story of Yusuf: his brothers wronged him, Allah raised him in Egypt, and he later forgave his brothers and provided for them. That story is a full surah, Surat Yusuf. You do not need every detail yet. You do need his name in the list, and the lesson that he remained truthful under hardship.

Qur’an 6:84-86 mentions Ibrahim’s descendants among the guided: Ishaq, Yaqub, and later Yusuf among other prophets. Write the eleven names you now have, from Adam to Yusuf, until you can say them without looking. The remaining fourteen come in the next lesson. Do not skip a name, because the outcome is to mention all twenty-five.

## Key words
• Khalilullah — the close friend of Allah, a title of Ibrahim (alayhis-salam)
• alayhis-salam — peace be upon him; said after a prophet’s name

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put these six names in the order used in class: Yusuf, Ibrahim, Ismail, Lut, Yaqub, Ishaq.

Working:
1. Ibrahim comes first among them.
2. Then Lut, then Ibrahim’s sons Ismail and Ishaq.
3. Then Yaqub, then Yusuf.

Answer: Ibrahim, Lut, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, Yusuf.

## Activity: Write the prophets from Adam to Yusuf
You will need: Notebook, Name cards for the eleven prophets
1. Arrange the cards from Adam to Yusuf.
2. Check the order with the verses your teacher points to in Qur’an 6:84-86 and with the class list.
3. Each learner writes the eleven names in the notebook.
4. Say the list aloud twice as a group.

## Practice
1. Who is called Khalilullah?
2. Name the two sons of Ibrahim included in the list of prophets.
3. Whose son was Yusuf?
4. Recite the eleven names from Adam to Yusuf in order.

## Summary
• Ibrahim, Lut, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub and Yusuf follow the first five prophets.
• Ismail and Ishaq were sons of Ibrahim, Yaqub was the son of Ishaq, and Yusuf was the son of Yaqub.
• The list from Adam to Yusuf has eleven names.

### Answers to practice
1. Ibrahim (alayhis-salam).
2. Ismail and Ishaq.
3. Yusuf was the son of Yaqub.
4. Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, Yusuf.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: From Ayyub to Muhammad (S.A.W.)
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: FROM AYYUB TO MUHAMMAD (S.A.W.)
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Name the prophets from Ayyub to Muhammad (S.A.W.).
• Recite all twenty-five names.
• Acknowledge belief in every prophet, with Muhammad as the last.

Curriculum outcomes: a) mention the twenty-five prophets of Allah (S.W.T.) in the Qur’an; d) acknowledge the belief in the prophets of Allah as a Pillar of Iman

## Introduction
The second half of the list includes Musa, Dawud, Sulayman, Isa and Muhammad (S.A.W.). When these fourteen names join the first eleven, the twenty-five are complete.

## Notes
### The remaining prophets
Continue the list in this order:

12. Ayyub
13. Shuayb
14. Musa
15. Harun
16. Dhul-Kifl
17. Dawud
18. Sulayman
19. Ilyas
20. Al-Yasa
21. Yunus
22. Zakariyya
23. Yahya
24. Isa
25. Muhammad (S.A.W.)

Musa (alayhis-salam) was sent to Fir’awn and was given the Tawrah. Allah spoke to him, as Qur’an 4:164 states. Harun was his brother and a prophet with him. Dawud was given the Zabur (Qur’an 4:163). Sulayman was the son of Dawud and a prophet-king. Yunus (alayhis-salam), also called Dhul-Nun, called on Allah from inside the fish. Zakariyya was the father of Yahya. Isa (alayhis-salam), the son of Maryam, is a prophet and messenger. He is not the son of Allah. Surat Al-Ikhlas has already taught that Allah does not beget.

Shuayb, Dhul-Kifl, Ilyas and Al-Yasa are also among the twenty-five. Do not drop their names because the stories are shorter in class.

### The full belief
Say the twenty-five names until they are firm. Believe in every one of them. Love them and follow the message as completed by Muhammad (S.A.W.). We say “alayhis-salam” after the earlier prophets and “Sallallahu alayhi wa sallam” after Muhammad. Rejecting Isa, or calling him God, both contradict this pillar. He is a honoured prophet of Allah, and Muhammad is the last messenger.

## Key words
• Tawrah — the scripture given to Musa (alayhis-salam)
• Zabur — the scripture given to Dawud (alayhis-salam)
• Sallallahu alayhi wa sallam — may Allah send prayers and peace upon him; said after the name of Prophet Muhammad

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A classmate says Isa is the son of Allah, and another says Isa was not a prophet. How does the list of twenty-five correct both sentences?

Working:
1. Isa is prophet number 24 in the class list. He is a true prophet.
2. Allah has no children, as Surat Al-Ikhlas teaches.
3. Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the twenty-fifth and the last.

Answer: Isa is a prophet of Allah, not His son. We believe in him and in Muhammad (S.A.W.) as the final prophet.

## Activity: Write all twenty-five names
You will need: Notebook, The references Qur’an 4:163-165, 6:84-86 and 21:85-88 as the teacher reads the names
1. Listen as the teacher reads the prophets named in those passages.
2. Write all twenty-five names in order in your notebook.
3. Cover the page and, in pairs, test each other on any five names.
4. End by stating that belief in all of them is a pillar of Iman and that Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last.

## Practice
1. Who was given the Tawrah, and who was given the Zabur?
2. Where does Isa stand in the list, and who comes after him?
3. Name Dhul-Kifl’s place among these prophets: is he included in the twenty-five?
4. How many prophets are in the full list?

## Summary
• The list ends with Ayyub, Shuayb, Musa, Harun, Dhul-Kifl, Dawud, Sulayman, Ilyas, Al-Yasa, Yunus, Zakariyya, Yahya, Isa and Muhammad (S.A.W.).
• There are twenty-five prophets to mention.
• We believe in all of them, and Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the seal of the prophets.

### Answers to practice
1. Musa was given the Tawrah, and Dawud was given the Zabur.
2. Isa is the twenty-fourth. Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the twenty-fifth and the last.
3. Yes. Dhul-Kifl is one of the twenty-five prophets.
4. Twenty-five.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Patience and obedience of the prophets
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: PATIENCE AND OBEDIENCE OF THE PROPHETS
================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain patience using the examples of Nuh and Ayyub.
• Explain obedience using Ibrahim and Yunus.
• Write the meaning of each virtue in a notebook sentence.

Curriculum outcomes: b) analyse the virtues of the prophets of Allah for character formation

## Introduction
The prophets were not guides only because of miracles. They were guides because of character. Two of their virtues are patience when the road is long, and obedience when the command is hard.

## Notes
### Patience
Sabr means staying firm on what is right, without giving up and without complaining against Allah. Nuh (alayhis-salam) called his people to Allah for a thousand years minus fifty, and most of them still refused (Qur’an 29:14). He did not abandon the message. Ayyub (alayhis-salam) was tested with serious illness and loss. He called on his Lord and remained patient. The Qur’an says Allah answered him and removed the harm (Qur’an 21:83-84).

Patience is not silence in the face of bullying that you should report. It is firmness: you keep praying, you keep telling the truth, and you do not insult Allah because a week has been difficult.

### Obedience
The prophets obeyed Allah even when the command cost them comfort. Ibrahim (alayhis-salam) was tested with a command about his son. The son, understanding the dream his father had been shown, said that his father should do what he was commanded, and Allah ransomed the son with a great sacrifice (Qur’an 37:102-107). That obedience is remembered at Eid al-Adha.

Yunus (alayhis-salam) left his people without waiting as he should have. He was swallowed by the fish. Inside it he obeyed by turning back to Allah with the words: there is no god but You, glory be to You, I have been among the wrongdoers (Qur’an 21:87). Allah saved him. Obedience includes coming back as soon as you know you were wrong.

Write both virtues in your own words and attach one prophet to each, so the story and the virtue stay together.

## Key words
• sabr — patience; remaining firm in obedience to Allah
• obedience — doing what Allah has commanded

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner has invited a classmate to salah for many days and feels like stopping. Which prophet’s patience speaks to this moment?

Working:
1. Nuh continued his call for a very long time.
2. The learner’s few days are small beside that patience.
3. He continues kindly, without insulting the classmate.

Answer: Nuh (alayhis-salam). The learner keeps inviting kindly and does not give up at once.

## Activity: Describe patience and obedience
You will need: Notebook, Verses read by the teacher: Qur’an 21:83-84, 21:87, 29:14 and 37:102-107
1. In pairs, describe the patience of Nuh and of Ayyub in two or three sentences.
2. Describe the obedience of Ibrahim and his son, and the return of Yunus to Allah.
3. Write the points in your notebook under the headings Patience and Obedience.
4. Read one point to the class.

## Practice
1. How did Ayyub show patience?
2. What did Yunus say when he turned back to Allah from inside the fish?
3. What virtue did Ibrahim and his son show when Ibrahim was tested?

## Summary
• Nuh and Ayyub are models of patience.
• Ibrahim and his son obeyed Allah in a hard test, and Yunus obeyed by turning back.
• Patience and obedience are virtues for character, not only stories.

### Answers to practice
1. He remained patient during serious illness and called on Allah, who removed the harm.
2. There is no god but You. Glory be to You. Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.
3. Obedience. The son told his father to do what Allah had commanded.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Honesty, truthfulness and generosity
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: HONESTY, TRUTHFULNESS AND GENEROSITY
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain honesty and truthfulness from the lives of the prophets.
• Explain generosity from Ibrahim and Muhammad (S.A.W.).
• Separate a true virtue from a similar bad habit.

Curriculum outcomes: b) analyse the virtues of the prophets of Allah for character formation

## Introduction
People trusted the prophets with news from Allah because the prophets did not lie about small things. They also gave freely. Honesty, truthfulness and generosity are the next virtues to learn.

## Notes
### Honesty and truthfulness
Honesty means dealing fairly: you do not steal, cheat in measure, or take a hidden advantage. Truthfulness means your words match the facts. All the prophets were truthful. Their people sometimes rejected the message, but they could not prove that the prophet was a liar in his character.

Muhammad (S.A.W.) was called As-Sadiq Al-Amin, the truthful and trustworthy, before prophethood. Yusuf (alayhis-salam) was trusted with the storehouses of Egypt because the king saw that he was knowledgeable and trustworthy. A prophet does not pass an exam by cheating or sell goods by hiding a fault.

### Generosity
Generosity is giving freely what is lawful to give. Ibrahim (alayhis-salam) hurried to prepare food when guests came to him (Qur’an 51:24-27). He did not wait to be pushed. Muhammad (S.A.W.) was the most generous of people, and he was even more generous in Ramadan (Bukhari). He did not love hoarding.

### Do not mix the virtue with a fault
Truthfulness is not the same as saying a hurtful thing for fun and then claiming “I was only honest”. Honesty does not cancel kindness. Generosity is not giving away someone else’s property, and it is not wasting. A generous learner shares a pencil, gives from what a parent allows, and still leaves enough for his or her own need. Write one clear sentence for each virtue so that you can use it in the role-play of the next lesson.

## Key words
• honesty — dealing fairly and not taking what is not yours
• truthfulness — saying what is true
• generosity — giving freely from what is lawful

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A seller of mangoes hides the rotten ones under the good ones. Which virtue of the prophets has he broken, and what would Yusuf’s example suggest?

Working:
1. Hiding a fault in a sale is dishonest.
2. The prophets were trustworthy in their dealings.
3. He should show the fruit as it is or remove the rotten ones.

Answer: He has broken honesty. A prophetic example is to deal in a way people can trust.

## Activity: Three virtues on paper
You will need: Notebook
1. In small groups, discuss honesty, truthfulness and generosity using the prophets named in the lesson.
2. Write one sentence for each virtue and one prophet beside it.
3. Add one school example that is really the virtue, and reject one example that only pretends to be.
4. Read your sentences to another group.

## Practice
1. What titles did people give Muhammad (S.A.W.) that show truthfulness and trust?
2. How did Ibrahim show generosity to his guests?
3. Why is sharing another person’s pencil without permission not generosity?

## Summary
• The prophets were honest and truthful, and people could trust their dealings.
• Ibrahim fed his guests quickly, and Muhammad (S.A.W.) was most generous, especially in Ramadan.
• Kind truthfulness and lawful giving are the real virtues.

### Answers to practice
1. As-Sadiq, the Truthful, and Al-Amin, the Trustworthy.
2. He hurried to prepare food for them.
3. Generosity gives what you may lawfully give. Taking someone else’s property is not giving.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Practising the virtues of the prophets
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: PRACTISING THE VIRTUES OF THE PROPHETS
================================================

## What you will learn
• Role-play patience, honesty, truthfulness, generosity and obedience.
• Choose one virtue to practise this week.
• State again that belief in the prophets is a pillar of Iman.

Curriculum outcomes: b) analyse the virtues of the prophets of Allah for character formation; c) apply the virtues of the prophets of Allah in their daily life; d) acknowledge the belief in the prophets of Allah as a Pillar of Iman

## Introduction
A virtue that stays inside a notebook has not yet formed character. The prophets’ patience, honesty, truthfulness, generosity and obedience are for the corridor, the market and the kitchen, not only for a test.

## Notes
### From story to action
Apply each virtue in a way that fits your age:

- Patience: keep learning a surah that is taking time. Do not tear the page or insult yourself. Ask for help and continue, as Nuh continued and as Ayyub remained firm.
- Obedience: do the halal thing your parent or teacher asks when it does not contradict Allah. If you slipped, return quickly, as Yunus returned to Allah with dua.
- Honesty: give back extra change. Do not hide a fault in something you sell or swap.
- Truthfulness: tell the teacher what actually happened when a window breaks. As-Sadiq did not invent a story.
- Generosity: share food or a skill. Explain a sum to a classmate who is stuck.

### Belief that changes behaviour
Acknowledging the prophets as a pillar of Iman means you mention all twenty-five with respect, you refuse to mock any of them, and you try to wear their virtues. Saying “I believe in Musa” while cheating, or “I love Ibrahim” while refusing to share, leaves the belief unfinished. The pillar is in the heart, and the virtues show it in the limbs.

Choose one virtue for seven days. Tell a partner the exact action. At the end of the week, be honest about whether you did it. If you failed on one day, obey Allah by starting again the next morning. That second start is itself a prophetic lesson.

## Key words
• apply — to put a virtue into a real action
• character formation — building steady good habits

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You accidentally break a friend’s ruler and feel like saying the desk broke it. Which virtue, and which prophetic title, correct you?

Working:
1. Truthfulness means the words match the facts.
2. The Prophet (S.A.W.) was As-Sadiq.
3. You apologise and offer to replace the ruler if you can.

Answer: Truthfulness, following As-Sadiq. Admit the break and make it right.

## Activity: Role-play the five virtues
You will need: Five situation cards: a hard surah, a parent’s lawful instruction, extra change, a broken ruler, a classmate without a pencil
1. In groups, pick one card and act the wrong response, then the prophetic response.
2. The class names the virtue: patience, obedience, honesty, truthfulness or generosity.
3. Each learner writes the virtue he or she will practise this week and the exact action.
4. Close by reciting the number of prophets, twenty-five, and stating that belief in them is a pillar of Iman.

## Practice
1. Give one way to practise patience with schoolwork.
2. Give one way to practise generosity without money.
3. Why is mocking any prophet against this pillar?
4. How many prophets must you be able to mention?

## Summary
• Patience, obedience, honesty, truthfulness and generosity can be practised at school.
• Belief in the prophets shows in respect for all twenty-five and in these virtues.
• If you fail one day, start again the next day.

### Answers to practice
1. Keep learning a difficult surah or sum, ask for help, and do not give up in anger.
2. Explain a lesson to a classmate or share time and learning materials.
3. Belief in all the prophets is a pillar of Iman, so every prophet is mentioned with respect.
4. Twenty-five.

questions.question: How many prophets are named in the list you learned?
questions.explanation: The Grade 4 list has twenty-five prophets, ending with Muhammad (S.A.W.).

questions.question: Who is the first prophet in the list, and who is the last?
questions.explanation: Adam is the first human and the first prophet. Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the seal of the prophets.

questions.question: Which statement about Isa (alayhis-salam) matches the pillar of Iman?
options: He is the son of Allah
He is a prophet of Allah, and Allah has no children
questions.explanation: Isa is honoured as a prophet. Surat Al-Ikhlas teaches that Allah does not beget.

questions.question: Who was given the Zabur?
questions.explanation: Qur’an 4:163 says Dawud was given the Zabur.

questions.question: Nuh’s long call to his people is an example of which virtue?
questions.explanation: He remained among them for a thousand years minus fifty and did not abandon the message.

questions.question: Ayyub (alayhis-salam) is remembered especially for patience during which test?
questions.answer: Serious illness, after which he called on Allah and Allah removed the harm.

questions.question: Ibrahim hurrying to feed his guests is an example of which virtue?
options: hiding a fault in a sale

questions.question: Which action applies truthfulness at school?
options: Blaming the desk for something you broke
Telling the teacher what really happened
Copying and saying the work is yours
questions.explanation: Truthfulness means your words match the facts, as in the title As-Sadiq.

questions.question: What does Yunus turning to Allah from inside the fish teach?
options: that a sin cannot be followed by dua
that the fish was a prophet
that we may leave every duty
questions.explanation: He admitted his fault and called on Allah, who saved him.

questions.question: Belief in the prophets means…
questions.answer: Believing in all twenty-five, respecting every one of them, and knowing that Muhammad (S.A.W.) is the last.
questions.explanation: This belief is a pillar of Iman.

questions.question: Which group is in the correct order?
questions.explanation: After Ibrahim come Lut, then Ismail and Ishaq, then Yaqub, then Yusuf. The option that keeps Ibrahim before his descendants is correct.
